title: Brandy and Cognac Hangover: Why It Hits Hard and How to Avoid It
excerpt: Why brandy and cognac hangovers feel so rough: congeners, grape methanol, VS vs XO, grappa and pisco, the after-dinner digestif trap, and how to sip smarter.
metaDescription: Why do brandy and cognac cause bad hangovers? Congeners, methanol, VS vs XO, grappa and pisco, and how to sip cognac without wrecking tomorrow.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, brandy and cognac have a reputation for rough hangovers, and it isn't only folklore. They belong to the group of dark, aged spirits that carry more congeners, the extra chemicals made during fermentation, distillation, and barrel aging. Grape and fruit brandies also tend to carry more methanol than grain spirits, because fruit skins contain pectin that breaks down into it. In a well-known 1970s comparison, brandy came out at the top of the list for hangover severity. But here is the part that matters most: **how much you drink matters far more than what you drink.** Three snifters of cognac after a bottle of wine at dinner will hurt no matter how fine the bottle was.

**The quick rules:** Count a cognac pour honestly (a standard drink is 1.5 oz, and a generous snifter is often 2 oz or more). Remember that brandy usually arrives at the end of a meal, after the wine, so it stacks on top of everything else. Drink a full glass of water with it. Skip the second digestif. Treat sweet brandy drinks like eggnog, Brandy Alexanders, and pisco sours as real drinks, because they hide the alcohol. And never drink homemade or unlabeled fruit brandy from an unknown source, because badly made fruit spirits can contain dangerous levels of methanol.

> **This is not medical advice.** A hangover is unpleasant but normally passes within a day. **Get help right away (call 911 in the US) if** someone is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover. **If you drank homemade, bootleg, or unlabeled fruit brandy** (moonshine, homemade rakia or similar) and later develop blurred or "snowfield" vision, severe headache, abdominal pain, or rapid breathing, treat it as an emergency and tell the doctors what you drank. Methanol poisoning often shows up 12 to 24 hours after drinking, and it is treatable when caught early. Poison Control in the US is **1-800-222-1222**.

## Why Brandy and Cognac Hangovers Feel Worse

Brandy is a spirit distilled from wine or fermented fruit. Cognac is a specific brandy made from white grapes in the Cognac region of western France, double-distilled in copper pot stills and aged in French oak. That production style is exactly what gives cognac its flavor, and it's also why it tends to leave more behind for your body to deal with.

### Congeners: the flavor compounds that may make hangovers worse

Ethanol is the main cause of a hangover. It dehydrates you, disrupts your sleep, irritates your stomach, and triggers an inflammatory response. Congeners are the supporting cast. They include:

- **Methanol**, a simpler alcohol your body converts into formaldehyde and formic acid
- **Fusel alcohols** (longer-chain alcohols such as isoamyl alcohol), which give spirits body and some of their "hot" notes
- **Aldehydes and esters**, which carry fruity and floral aromas
- **Compounds pulled from the oak barrel**, such as tannins, vanillin, and furfural

Clear, highly purified spirits like vodka have very few congeners. Dark, aged spirits like bourbon, dark rum, and brandy have many more. Our full guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) goes deeper on what each type does.

### The methanol question

Brandy has a specific congener issue that sets it apart from whiskey: methanol. Grains have little pectin, but grapes and other fruits have a lot of it, especially in the skins. During fermentation, enzymes break pectin down and release methanol. Distillation concentrates it along with the ethanol.

The amounts in properly made commercial brandy are far below dangerous levels. Regulators in the EU and elsewhere set maximum methanol limits for fruit spirits, and reputable producers stay within them. The concern is about hangovers, not poisoning. Some researchers have proposed that methanol plays a role in the hangover because your body processes ethanol first and only gets around to methanol later, once ethanol levels fall. That would fit with the morning-after timing of a hangover. It's an interesting theory, but it hasn't been nailed down, so treat it as a possible contributor rather than the full explanation.

### What the barrel adds

Cognac must age in oak for at least two years, and older grades spend much longer in the barrel. Oak gives cognac its color, its vanilla and spice notes, and its smoothness. It also adds wood-derived compounds to the spirit. Aging does mellow some harsh compounds through slow oxidation, but on balance a barrel-aged spirit carries a heavier congener load than a clear, unaged one.

## What the Research Actually Says

The research on spirits and hangovers is small and mostly old, but it points in a consistent direction.

**The classic ranking.** A study by G.L.S. Pawan published in the *Proceedings of the Nutrition Society* in 1973 compared hangover effects across several drinks given at the same alcohol dose. Brandy ranked highest for hangover severity, with red wine, rum, whisky, white wine, gin, and vodka following. This ranking gets repeated all over the internet. It's worth knowing that it is a single, small study from five decades ago, so it's a hint rather than a final answer.

**Bourbon versus vodka.** A better-designed study by Damaris Rohsenow and colleagues, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010, gave healthy young adults either bourbon or vodka to a fairly high blood alcohol level, then measured them the next morning. People rated their hangovers as worse after bourbon, which has far more congeners. Interestingly, next-day performance on attention and reaction-time tasks was impaired by alcohol in general, and the type of spirit made little difference there. Bourbon isn't brandy, but it's the closest well-studied stand-in for a dark, aged, high-congener spirit.

**The takeaway.** The research supports the idea that high-congener spirits can make a hangover feel worse at the same amount of alcohol. It does not suggest that switching spirits will save you from the main effects of drinking too much. The alcohol itself does most of the damage.

## Brandy vs. Cognac vs. Armagnac: Is One Easier on You?

All cognac is brandy, but not all brandy is cognac. The differences in how they're made can affect how much flavor, and how many congeners, end up in your glass.

| Type | How it's made | Congener load (general) |
|---|---|---|
| Cognac | Grape wine, double pot-distilled, aged at least 2 years in French oak | High |
| Armagnac | Grape wine, usually single continuous distillation at a lower strength, oak-aged | High, often richer than cognac |
| Spanish brandy (Brandy de Jerez) | Grape spirit aged in sherry casks using a solera system | High, often sweeter |
| American / mass-market brandy | Often column-distilled to a lighter style, shorter aging | Moderate to high |
| Pisco | Grape brandy from Peru or Chile; Peruvian pisco is unaged and not diluted with water | Moderate to high |
| Grappa | Distilled from grape pomace (skins, seeds, stems) | High, with more methanol |
| Calvados, slivovitz, kirsch | Distilled from apples, plums, or cherries | High, with more methanol |

These are general patterns, not lab measurements for any particular bottle. Producers vary a lot. Still, a few things hold up:

- **Distilling to a lower strength keeps more congeners.** Armagnac is traditionally distilled to a lower alcohol level than cognac, which is one reason it tastes so full. More flavor in the spirit usually means more congeners.
- **Pot stills keep more character than column stills.** Big industrial column stills can strip out more of the extras, so lighter commercial brandies may be slightly gentler than an old Armagnac. "Slightly" is the key word.
- **Added sugar and sweet casks add their own problems.** Sweet brandies are easy to drink quickly, and sugar may make it harder to notice how much alcohol you've had.

## VS, VSOP, or XO: Does Expensive Cognac Mean a Milder Hangover?

Cognac grades are based on minimum aging time for the youngest spirit in the blend:

- **VS (Very Special):** at least 2 years in oak
- **VSOP (Very Superior Old Pale):** at least 4 years
- **XO (Extra Old):** at least 10 years

People often assume a pricey XO will be "cleaner." There's no good evidence that it is. Longer time in the barrel generally means more wood-derived compounds, not fewer. Cognac rules also allow small additions of caramel coloring, sugar, and oak extract to adjust color and taste, and these show up across grades.

What expensive cognac does do is encourage slower drinking. Few people throw back an XO. If a better bottle makes you sip one small pour over an hour instead of three quick ones, that will help far more than anything in the bottle itself. The price tag is not a hangover remedy, but the pace that often comes with it can be.

## Grappa Hangover: Why the Clear Stuff Isn't "Clean"

Grappa is an Italian spirit made from pomace, the skins, seeds, and stems left over after grapes are pressed for wine. Many grappas are clear and unaged, which leads people to assume they behave like vodka. They don't.

Pomace is exactly where most of a grape's pectin lives, so pomace spirits tend to have more methanol than brandy made from wine. EU spirit rules reflect this by allowing pomace spirits a higher methanol limit than many other categories. Grappa also keeps plenty of aromatic fusel alcohols and esters, which is why it can taste so intense and so "hot."

A few grappa-specific points:

- **Clear does not mean low-congener.** Color comes from barrel aging. A clear grappa skipped the barrel but is still full of fermentation and distillation congeners.
- **It's often strong.** Many grappas are bottled at 40% to 50% alcohol or higher. A small glass can be more than one standard drink.
- **It's usually served after a big meal.** Like cognac, grappa tends to arrive after wine, as a digestif or poured into an espresso (caffè corretto). The coffee doesn't sober you up, and it can make you feel more alert than you really are.

If grappa reliably wrecks your next day, it may be the combination of what came before plus a high-methanol, high-strength spirit at the end of the night.

## Pisco Hangover: The Pisco Sour Trap

Pisco is a grape brandy from Peru and Chile. Peruvian pisco has strict rules: it's distilled to bottling strength with no added water, and it isn't aged in wood. Chilean pisco can be diluted and can be aged. Some pisco is made from aromatic grapes such as Italia and Torontel, which carry strong floral notes.

Because Peruvian pisco is clear and unaged, it carries fewer barrel compounds than cognac. But it's still a grape spirit, so it still contains grape-derived methanol and fermentation congeners. It sits somewhere in the middle of the hangover range, not at the vodka end.

The bigger pisco problem is usually the **pisco sour**. It's made with about 2 oz of pisco, lime juice, sugar syrup, and frothy egg white. It tastes light and citrusy, the sugar and foam soften the alcohol, and it's easy to drink two or three without noticing that each one holds more than a standard drink. Add a hot day, a long lunch, or high altitude in the Andes, where many travelers feel the effects of alcohol faster, and you have a recipe for a rough morning.

If you're drinking pisco sours, count each one as at least one and a third drinks, alternate with water, and eat with them.

## Homemade and Fruit Brandies: The One Real Safety Warning

Fruit brandies like calvados (apple), slivovitz (plum), kirsch (cherry), and palinka or rakia are part of many food cultures. Commercially made versions are regulated and safe to drink in moderation, though they're high in congeners and methanol compared with grain spirits.

**Homemade and bootleg fruit spirits are different.** When fruit spirits are distilled carelessly, without discarding the first part of the run where methanol concentrates, or when illegal spirits are deliberately cut with industrial alcohol, methanol can reach toxic levels. Outbreaks of methanol poisoning from illicit spirits are reported around the world, including among travelers.

Methanol poisoning is not a bad hangover. It typically starts like being drunk, then after a delay of many hours causes vision problems (blurred, hazy, or "snowfield" vision), severe headache, stomach pain, vomiting, and fast breathing. It can cause permanent blindness and death, but hospitals can treat it effectively if they act early. If you drank an unknown homemade spirit and feel this way, go to the emergency room and tell them what you drank.

## The Digestif Problem: Brandy Usually Comes Last

Brandy's hangover reputation probably has as much to do with *when* people drink it as *what* it is.

Cognac, Armagnac, grappa, and calvados are classic after-dinner drinks. By the time the snifter comes out, many people have already had a cocktail before dinner and several glasses of wine with it. The brandy is the final push. That timing creates a few problems:

- **It's the last drink, so it's closest to bedtime.** Alcohol close to sleep fragments the second half of the night, which is a major cause of next-day fatigue.
- **Snifter pours are hard to judge.** A large, round glass makes a 2 oz or 3 oz pour look small. Many home pours of cognac are two standard drinks or more.
- **Mixing wine and brandy piles up congeners.** Red wine is itself a high-congener drink. Red wine followed by brandy combines two of the drinks that ranked worst in the old Pawan study. Our [wine hangover guide](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide) explains why wine nights hit hard on their own.
- **The order isn't the issue, the total is.** You may have heard "beer before liquor, never sicker." Research doesn't support the idea that the order of drinks matters. What matters is the total amount of alcohol. Our article on the [beer-before-liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) covers this.

## Brandy Cocktails That Sneak Up on You

Brandy shows up in several drinks that taste gentler than they are:

- **Eggnog and Tom and Jerry:** rich, sweet, and creamy, often served from a big bowl with no clear count of what's in your cup
- **Brandy Alexander:** cream, chocolate liqueur, and brandy, which means two alcohol sources in one dessert-like drink
- **Sidecar:** cognac plus orange liqueur, so again two spirits in one glass
- **Sangria:** wine with brandy added, which stacks a high-congener wine with a high-congener spirit
- **Brandy Old Fashioned:** a strong, mostly spirit drink that goes down smoothly with sugar and fruit

None of these are dangerous in themselves. The trick is to recognize that each one can be the equivalent of one and a half to two standard drinks, and count accordingly.

## How Brandy Compares With Other Spirits

Here is a rough guide, based on typical congener content and the limited research available. It's a tendency, not a guarantee, and your own experience may differ.

| Drink | General congener level | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Vodka | Very low | Closest to "just ethanol." See our guide to [vodka for fewer hangovers](/never-hungover/best-vodka-for-no-hangover). |
| Gin | Low | Botanicals add flavor but few heavy congeners |
| Blanco tequila (100% agave) | Low to moderate | Unaged, but agave adds its own compounds |
| Bourbon and whiskey | High | Well studied; see our [whiskey hangover guide](/never-hungover/whiskey-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) |
| Dark rum | High | See our [rum hangover guide](/never-hungover/rum-hangover) |
| Brandy and cognac | High | Barrel compounds plus grape methanol |
| Grappa and fruit brandies | High | Typically the most methanol among commercial spirits |

If you get noticeably worse hangovers from cognac than from vodka at the same amount, that's consistent with the research. Switching to a clearer spirit may help a little. Drinking less will help a lot.

## How to Enjoy Cognac Without Wrecking Tomorrow

You don't have to give up a good brandy. A few habits make a real difference:

1. **Measure the pour.** Use 1.5 oz (about 45 ml) as one standard drink. If you're pouring at home, a jigger keeps it honest.
2. **Make it the only digestif.** If you've already had wine, one small brandy is plenty. Skip the second round of grappa and the "one more" calvados.
3. **Sip it slowly.** Cognac is meant to be sipped over a long time. A single pour that lasts 30 to 45 minutes gives your body time to keep up.
4. **Have a glass of water alongside it.** Alcohol increases urine output. Water won't prevent a hangover by itself, but dehydration makes the headache and fatigue worse.
5. **Finish earlier.** Try to have your last drink a couple of hours before bed so your sleep is less disrupted.
6. **Don't drink on an empty stomach.** Brandy after a meal is better than brandy instead of a meal. Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood.
7. **Stick to reputable, labeled bottles.** This is the one rule that's about safety rather than comfort.

For a complete, evidence-based routine, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## If You Already Have a Cognac Hangover

There's no instant cure. Your body needs time to clear the alcohol and its by-products. You can make the wait easier:

- **Drink water or an electrolyte drink** steadily through the morning rather than all at once.
- **Eat something simple.** Toast, eggs, bananas, or a broth-based soup are easy on the stomach and help steady your blood sugar.
- **Treat the headache carefully.** Ibuprofen or naproxen can help, but take them with food because alcohol has already irritated your stomach. Be cautious with acetaminophen (Tylenol) after heavy drinking because of the extra load on the liver. Our [hangover headache relief guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) covers the options.
- **Rest.** A short nap and an early night will often do more than any remedy.
- **Skip "hair of the dog."** Another drink only delays the hangover and adds to the total.

If you feel much worse than a usual hangover, can't keep fluids down, or notice any vision changes after drinking an unknown spirit, see the warning box at the top of this page.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people who enjoy dark spirits add a DHM (dihydromyricetin) supplement to their routine. DHM is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree, studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's best viewed as promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that DHM can offset heavy drinking or make a high-congener night consequence-free, and it does nothing about methanol in unsafe spirits.

If you want to try it alongside the habits above, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Brandy and cognac are high-congener spirits, with barrel compounds and more grape-derived methanol than grain spirits. At the same amount of alcohol, they may give you a worse hangover than vodka or gin.
- The research is limited: one old study ranked brandy worst, and a better modern study found that a high-congener spirit (bourbon) produced worse hangovers than vodka.
- Expensive cognac is not "cleaner." It can only help by encouraging you to sip slowly.
- Grappa and fruit brandies tend to carry the most methanol. Pisco sits in the middle, but pisco sours hide their strength.
- The biggest factor is total alcohol. Brandy usually comes after wine, so the digestif is often what tips the night over.
- Never drink homemade or unlabeled fruit spirits from unknown sources, and treat vision changes after drinking as an emergency.

For how this drink compares with the rest, see our [ranking of alcohol from least to most hangover](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) and our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does brandy give you a worse hangover than other drinks?**

It can. Brandy is a dark, barrel-aged spirit with more congeners than clear spirits, and grape brandies also contain more methanol than grain spirits. A 1973 study ranked brandy highest for hangover severity at the same alcohol dose, and a 2010 study found a high-congener spirit (bourbon) caused worse hangovers than vodka. Still, the total amount of alcohol matters far more than the type.

**Why does cognac give me such a bad hangover?**

Usually it's a combination of things. Cognac is high in congeners from fermentation and oak aging, it contains some grape-derived methanol, and it's usually poured at the end of a night that already included wine or cocktails. Generous snifter pours are often two standard drinks or more, and drinking close to bedtime disrupts sleep, which makes the next day feel worse.

**Is XO cognac less likely to cause a hangover than VS?**

There's no good evidence that it is. XO spends longer in oak than VS, which generally means more wood-derived compounds, not fewer. The one advantage of a fine cognac is that people tend to sip it slowly, and drinking more slowly and drinking less is what actually reduces a hangover.

**Does grappa cause bad hangovers?**

Grappa often does, for people who are sensitive to congeners. It's distilled from grape skins, seeds, and stems, which are rich in pectin, so pomace spirits typically contain more methanol than other brandies. Many grappas are also strong and served after a big meal with wine. Being clear does not make it low in congeners.

**Is pisco less likely to give you a hangover?**

Peruvian pisco is unaged, so it carries fewer barrel compounds than cognac, but it's still a grape brandy with fermentation congeners and some methanol. It falls in the middle of the range. The bigger risk is the pisco sour: each one holds about 2 oz of pisco, and the sugar and egg white make it easy to drink several quickly.

**What is the difference between brandy and cognac?**

Brandy is any spirit distilled from wine or fermented fruit. Cognac is a specific type of grape brandy made in the Cognac region of France, double-distilled in copper pot stills and aged at least two years in French oak. All cognac is brandy, but most brandy is not cognac.

**Is homemade fruit brandy dangerous?**

It can be. Fruit spirits naturally contain more methanol, and careless home distillation or illegal spirits cut with industrial alcohol can reach toxic levels. Methanol poisoning often starts hours after drinking with blurred vision, severe headache, stomach pain, and fast breathing. If that happens, get emergency care right away and tell the doctors what you drank. In the US, Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222.

**How can I drink cognac without getting a hangover?**

No method guarantees a hangover-free morning, but you can reduce the odds. Measure your pour (1.5 oz is one standard drink), make it your only digestif after wine, sip it slowly, drink water alongside it, finish a couple of hours before bed, and don't drink on an empty stomach.
